abstractText:
This collaborative project comprised of ten awards will integrate information about bryophytes and lichens, with each other and with their commensal organisms, including fungi, on a worldwide scale. Bryophytes and lichens are functionally related as the main hosts for cryptobiotic communities forming minute "forests" that provide a matrix of habitats for many microscopic organisms, including tardigrades, mites, rotifers, micro-mollusks, microalgae, microfungi, and prokaryotes. These communities have global relevance and perform essential functions on our planet, for example, the biological soil crusts that harbor these communities form a "living skin" covering approximately 12% of  Earth's terrestrial surface.  In addition, professional training will be provided for a large number of undergraduates, with a focus on leveraging local resources to promote underrepresented students in STEM fields.  Students will be trained in digitization and collections management, and will contribute to the education and public outreach components of the project. 

Through this collaboration, twenty-five US herbaria will image and digitize associated metadata for almost 1.2 million bryophyte and lichen herbarium specimens held in US institutions. Imaging the physical specimens of these organisms and integrating data from comparative genomics, nucleotide sequence data, and other resources is unprecedented on this scale. These integrated data will form a critical resource for evolutionary and ecological studies, that may, in turn, lead to a deeper understanding of (1) how biocrusts perform their ecosystem functions, (2) the roles of bryophytes and lichens in carbon/nitrogen cycling, (3) the dynamic evolution of symbioses in space and time, (4) the historical and contemporary drivers of endophyte co-diversification, and (5) the evolution of biodiversity using spatial phylogenetics. Deep-learning approaches using repurposed digital images may also provide powerful new investigative tools.  Digitized data will be shared with iDigBio.org and other repositories.  A multi-pronged approach to broader impacts spans from K-12 to participatory citizen science initiatives.  These include (1) diverse digital, interactive, and object-based learning outreach programs; (2) online lesson plans; (3) science youth groups; (4) Science Clubs and public educator workshops; and (5) a series of videos using Learning Glass – which collapses the perspectives of viewer and presenter into one shared perspective. In addition, the PIs and collaborating institutions will host WeDigBio and K-12 clubs hosting label transcription crowdsourcing events during the award period. The project also partners with Zooniverse, leaders in online citizen science, where we will develop an online platform for citizen scientists to make observations on character traits that can then enhance metadata not always on the scientific label data.

projectOutComesReport:
The Wisconsin State Herbarium (WIS) at the University of Wisconsin-Madison fully digitized >46,000 historical specimens of lichens, mosses, hornworts, and liverworts from its collection for this collaborative effort.  This included imaging of >30,000 specimens.  WIS also served as the centralized georeferencing center for this national network and processed material from several partner institutions, including the Bishop Museum in Hawaii.  As a result, we helped to establish a novel consortium for understudied nonvascular plants and lichens that combined information about the morphology and geographic distribution of these symbiotic organisms that are important drivers of ecological change and ecosystem processes.  The data generated for this project, including tens of thousands of high resolution images, now reside in two fully open-access Symbiota portals (lichenportal.org and bryophyteportal.org), which are among the most heavily used among thematic collections networks.  In conjunction with the creation of these public tools, we also focused on public engagement and education by creating a set of educational videos that feature graduate students affiliated with WIS.  These have been shared on YouTube and other online platforms for teachers and citizens.  Over the course of the grant period WIS employed an exceptional team of professionals and students, both graduate and undergraduate, who received on-the-job training in natural history museum curation, data processing, and digital technology.  In this way they improved their scientific skills to unlock data from digital images of specimens and to connect digitization and natural history collections to biology education and the general public.

abstractText:
Electron paramagnetic resonance imaging (EPRI) is a low-cost and highly specific imaging technique with significant applications. In medical imaging, EPRI can be used to obtain tissue oxygenation images to identify oxygen-starved areas of tissue. Oxygen-starved areas of cancer are usually more aggressive and harder to treat, so a medical imaging tool to identify hypoxia would be highly useful. A primary advantage of EPRI relative to other medical imaging techniques is the significantly lower cost of its instrumentation. For example, in comparison to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), EPRI can be performed without using a superconducting magnet. This drastically reduces the cost of constructing, siting, and operating EPRI systems compared to MRI systems. Unlike MRI, however, the technology for using EPRI to perform whole-body human imaging has not yet been developed. One of the primary challenges in further development of EPRI is the difficulty in performing signal excitation at the frequency ranges that are desirable for high-sensitivity imaging. This project addresses this shortcoming by developing novel instrumentations that will ultimately enable EPRI systems to be used for whole-body human imaging. The successful completion of this project has the potential for the development of a low-cost, human imaging technology. Since this technology offers imaging capabilities similar to MRI but at a small fraction of its cost it is expected to   significantly reduce the cost of medical diagnostic techniques based on imaging technologies.  This will likely contribute towards reducing the cost of overall healthcare services provided to the public in the U.S. and around the world. Additionally, this project has important educational impacts, which include increased participation of under-represented students in research and graduate engineering education, active involvement of undergraduate students in research, mentoring K-12 science teachers and curriculum development, and broad dissemination of research results to the public.

The overall objective of this project is to develop new techniques for continuous-wave (CW) electron paramagnetic resonance imaging (EPRI) that enhance its sensitivity and move towards the development of instrumentation capable of whole-body human imaging. Specifically, we propose to develop a traveling-wave (TW) approach for continuous-wave electron-paramagnetic resonance imaging. In the TW approach, RF signal excitation is performed using traveling waves that propagate from a remote antenna or probe inside a waveguide through tissue. In comparison to the conventional reactive near field approach, uniform magnetic fields across a much larger volume can be realized using the TW approach. Therefore, the development of the continuous-wave, TW-EPRI is expected to enable both the necessary volumetric coverage and sufficiently high magnetic field strength needed to perform whole-body human imaging. To accomplish this, we will pursue four aims to develop and study novel, low-cost CW, TW-EPRI instrumentation. These include: 1) develop a CW, traveling-wave EPRI system in a parallel plate waveguide environment to demonstrate feasibility for a traveling wave EPRI system; 2) Develop phased-array transmit techniques for improved magnetic field uniformity in high-frequency (>300 MHz) continuous-wave, TW-EPRI systems; 3) Integrate the imaging system and develop improved reconstruction algorithms; and 4) Develop techniques for accelerating image acquisition speed and improving the sensitivity of CW, TW-EPRI systems.

projectOutComesReport:
The traveling-wave electron paramagnetic resonance imaging (TW-EPRI) is a technology that offers imaging capabilities similar to MRI but at a small fraction of its cost. This can potentially reduce the cost of medical diagnostic techniques of novel imaging technologies and contribute towards reducing the cost of the healthcare services provided to the public in the U.S. and around the world. The TW-EPRI technology offers the ability to non-invasively obtain in vivo tissue measurements such as oxygenation, pH, redox status, and exposure to ionizing radiation. This has significant applications toward human health in a wide range of diseases such as cancer, heart disease, stroke, and ischemic limb disease. The key outcomes of this project are listed below:

 

1)      Development of a continuous-wave, traveling-wave electron paramagnetic resonance imaging in a cylindrical waveguide environment at 1 GHz. We developed a new architecture for a TW-EPRI system consisting of a circular waveguide fed with one or more monopole antennas used to generate a uniform magnetic field distribution in its interior region at a frequency of nearly 1 GHz. The system uses one or more receiver coils to perform electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) imaging in a transmission mode in which the high-frequency magnetic field component of the traveling wave electromagnetic wave generated by the waveguide is received and sensed by the receiver coils. The entire system is placed in a larger water-cooled electromagnet whose intensity can be changed to create the appropriate EPR resonance conditions within the object to be measured. A pair of Helmholtz coils are used to modulate the intensity of this dc magnetic field in the vicinity of the object to be imaged to simplify the task of isolating the desired signal from system noise using a lock-in amplifier. We also developed the complete RF transceiver chain used for transmitting the signal and receiving the modulated EPR signal of the sample and demonstrated that this system can successfully perform electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy in the traveling wave mode at a frequency of 1 GHz. 

 

2)      Integration of the TW-EPR imaging system with gradient coils for three-dimensional imaging. We converted the traveling-wave EPR spectroscopy system described above to a three-dimensional EPR imaging system by integrating the system with a set of gradient coils that allow us to sweep the intensity of the magnetic field in three dimensions and thus localize the region from which the EPR signal is being measured. This enables the system to acquire two-dimensional images of a three-dimensional object in different cut planes that can be controlled at will. Fig. 1 shows a photograph of the main components of this system including the circular waveguide and the gradient coils. Fig. 2 shows a few sample two-dimensional images obtained from this system in different cut planes. In this imaging experiment, the imaging object or phantom consisted of two vials with a diameter of 3 mm containing a powder with sufficient free radicals to have a measurable electron paramagnetic resonance signal.

 

Broader impacts:

The broader impacts of the educational activities conducted in this project include the research-based training and education of graduate and undergraduate students. This work supported the education of two graduate students one of whom completed his M.S. degree in April 2023 and is currently working towards his Ph.D. degree on the same topic. The other graduate student is expected to receive an M.S. degree in Fall of 2024 while continuing to work towards a Ph.D. degree. Both of these Ph.D. students are making excellent progress towards receiving their Ph.D. degrees. Using an REU supplement received for this project, the project also supported the undergraduate research-based educational activities of four undergraduate students. Of these students, two of them continued to pursue advanced graduate level studies after graduating with their B.S. degrees. The findings of this project were also broadly disseminated through the publication of conference papers.

abstractText:
Plants are anchored in place but can move and grow in response to the physical environment. One such remarkable response is to gravity: regardless of the position of the plant, whether turned upside down or sideways, young plant roots will grow in the direction of gravity, towards the Earth and shoots will grow away from gravity, in the direction of light.  How the plant perceives and responds to gravity stimulation is a question that has intrigued scientists a century and a half, since the time of Darwin. It is now known that variations in cell growth drive the movement of roots, but the growth patterns are subtle and complicated. Recently it was discovered that during the gravity response, roots grow down by curving and also self-straightening, a mechanically puzzling but essential phenomenon related to how the roots acquire water and nutrients from the soil. This project investigates how self-straightening occurs using interdisciplinary methods, including novel imaging techniques, mathematics, molecular genetics and genomics. The long-term goal is to identify the genes that control the curving root response to gravity. Understanding how roots grow into and through the soil will open the door to manipulating and selecting for more efficient root growth.  As the world faces changing water availability and deficits, this research could uncover root responses that can be harnessed for crop improvements. The project also brings the wonder of plant movement to the general public through establishing museum displays complete with images and information about root growth. Graduate and undergraduate students will be trained in inter-disciplinary biological research to help move these studies into the future.

Plant organs have the ability to sense a curvature and respond by straightening, a process that is evocative of proprioception. This auto-straightening response contributes to organ's posture, an important determinant of overall plant architecture, productivity and market value. When gravistimulated, Brachypodium roots initially respond by developing a strong downward curvature whose rate decreases after the tip reaches a 45-degree angle from the vertical. At this point, the root straightens before undergoing a new round of curvature. This process reiterates several times before the tip reaches a vertical posture. From then on, the root tip continues to oscillate around the vertical. A mathematical model was built to recapitulate these complex behaviors, and used to estimate explanatory parameters of the movements for a total of 46 distinct Brachypodium accessions. This allowed the development of a genome-wide association study (GWAS) aimed at identifying contributing genes. Several DNA polymorphisms were found to be associated with the amplitude of the oscillations. The main objective of this project is to investigate the cellular characteristics of these oscillations, and study the molecular mechanisms controlling them. The specific aims are: 1) Characterize the spatio-temporal distribution of curvatures and accompanying auto-straightening phases during a graviresponse; 2) Investigate the involvement of auxin gradients in their regulation, and 3) Initiate a molecular characterization of these oscillations, using transcriptomics and GWAS approaches to identify candidate regulators. These experiments will lead to a better understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms that govern auto-straightening and proprioception in plants.

projectOutComesReport:
Roots play critical roles in plant growth, development and reproduction by anchoring the plant into the soil and acquiring water and nutrients for the entire organism. To do so, they typically grow downward into the soil where they use a variety of directional cues for guidance. However, soils also interfere with root growth, either because of compaction by heavy equipment used in modern agricultural practices, climate impact and/or presence of rocks, pebbles and/or gravel. An oscillatory growth movement of the root tip named circumnutation was previously hypothesized to facilitate soil penetration and obstacle avoidance. However, the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control this behavior remain poorly understood. In this project, we used Brachypodium distachyon, a model monocot plant closely related to major cultivated crops such as oat, wheat and barley, to characterize the cellular mechanisms that drive this complex movement and identify molecular pathways that contribute to its regulation.

We initially used time-lapse photography to evaluate Brachypodium root-tip circumnutation following plant reorientation within the gravity field.  Computer-driven image analysis identified a region of the root tip where gravitropic and circumnutation curvatures initiate, and another region farther away from the tip where an auto-straightening response follows. This process reiterates itself, with successive leftward and rightward curvatures, resulting in an oscillatory movement with a ~125-min period (Figure 1). This movement is amenable to mathematical modeling, and a collaboration with Professor Shih-Hao Su from the Chinese Culture University in Taiwan led to the development of a software package (FROG) that extracts the period and amplitude of circumnutation from time-lapse images. This analysis revealed dramatic differences in circumnutation amplitude between Brachypodium accessions, and genetic investigations led to the identification of chromosomal loci associated with this parameter, including one on chromosome 2 that carries a candidate regulator also involved in the modulation of shoot internode size and tillering. Importantly, we were able to test accessions with distinct circumnutation amplitudes for their ability to penetrate gravel (Figure 2). Preliminary results indicate a correlation between root circumnutation amplitude and gravel penetrability.

To better understand localized features of root tip circumnutation, we again collaborated with Professor Su to develop a novel software package (TOAD) that features a user-friendly platform to capture time-lapse photographs of growing roots and analyze them using an AI-based image segmentation method. The algorithm automatically calculates dynamic features associated with root growth, tip angle and curvatures along the root midline and its edges. This package will allow a careful and automated evaluation of root growth and circumnutation parameters at high spatio-temporal resolution, giving valuable insights into this process.

In addition to the population genetics approach described above, we also initiated an analysis of root-tip expression profiles to evaluate the changes in gene expression that occur between phases of circumnutation. This investigation led to the discovery of a family of related genes whose expression increases in the root tip during the auto-straightening and second-curvature phases of circumnutation. Some of these differentially expressed genes encode proteins that bind to cellular microtubules, a cytoskeletal network that modulates the pattern of cell-wall material deposition, anisotropic cell expansion and general growth behavior. Transgenic plants over-expressing these genes take on a turfgrass-like appearance (Figure 3), suggesting novel strategies to engineer cover-crops for improved agricultural sustainability and soil protection against erosion.

More broadly, this project also allowed the development of science-education and outreach tools aimed at informing children and the general-public on the complex growth behaviors displayed by plant organs in response to environmental cues, and their potential implications for agriculture, horticulture and forestry. A slide-puzzle and flip-book plant-root kits were designed with distinct levels of complexity, tested in local libraries and museums, and improved.  A total of 500 optimized flipbook kits were then distributed to local libraries and children’s museums across Wisconsin. The Root Growth Flip Book was presented by Angela Johnson, its creator, at the 2025 Wisconsin Science Festival, and it was featured in Grow magazine.

Overall, this project allowed the training and professional development of one level-I scientist, one outreach specialist, one Masters’ student, one PhD student, seven undergraduate students and one high-school student. Four of the undergraduate students graduated with BS degrees and three of them joined competitive graduate programs after graduation. The PhD student is set to graduate in the spring of 2026 whereas the Master’s student graduated in 2022. This project led to two publications in peer-reviewed journals, three publications currently in preparation, and multiple research presentations delivered at national and international conferences. Two software packages (FROG and TOAD) have been developed and will be deposited in GitHub after publication.

abstractText:
This grant supports research that creates new understanding and capabilities regarding a manufacturing process enabling the fabrication of patterns and features on surfaces that are extremely small -- only a few billionths of a meter (a few nanometers) in extent. Precision fabrication at these lengths is driving manufacturing advances in areas of national importance including microelectronics, optical materials, sensors, chemical purification membranes, and quantum materials. This award supports fundamental research on block copolymer-based nanofabrication. When two different conventional polymers that do not “like” each other are mixed, the two polymers separate – like oil and water. However, when these two polymers are bonded to each other – to form a block copolymer – macroscopic separation is inhibited, and nanoscale segregation occurs instead. Features smaller than hundred (100), ten (10), and even five (5) nanometers are generated automatically, that cannot be easily created otherwise. This project focuses on spatially directing this nanoscale segregation on surfaces so that rationally organized and useful (as opposed to random) patterns can be formed. An example is nanopatterning the surfaces of semiconductors for computer chips so that they perform faster, are more energy efficient, and can be more complex. The research integrates advanced concepts from materials science and engineering, chemistry, and nanomanufacturing. The interdisciplinary research helps widen the involvement of diverse groups in fundamental research and constructively influences science and engineering education.

This research specifically addresses the challenge of registering and directing the self-assembly of vertically oriented block copolymer lamellar domains into rationally controlled sub-lithographic patterns through the exploitation of boundary-directed epitaxy. Boundary-directed epitaxy uses the abrupt chemical contrast that is inherent at spatial boundaries between regions on a substrate with different surface composition to direct the registration, alignment, and self-assembly of block copolymers. The advantages are substantial: the boundaries can be defined between features that are planar and relatively large – circumventing the need for trenches or high-resolution chemical patterns. The mechanisms that drive self-assembly are highly unexplored. The project determines the chemical composition / preferentiality window for boundary-directed epitaxy; quantifies the impact of boundary-roughness on assembly; characterizes how defects arise; and understands how the assembly evolves over time. The project studies and demonstrates boundary-directed epitaxy for nanofabrication, materials synthesis, and nanolithography; investigates assembly on templates with curved boundaries and complex shapes – essential for many applications; and, broadens the library of template materials that can be exploited to advance the generality of the phenomenon.

projectOutComesReport:
Lithography, the process used to create the tiny features that make up computer chips, drives progress in semiconductor technology. As desired feature sizes shrink, lithography tools have become increasingly complex and expensive in order to meet demands. However, even the most advanced systems face limitations in cost, edge roughness, and placement accuracy. Block copolymers, composed of two covalently linked yet mutually repelling (“immiscible”) polymer chains, are a promising alternative. This intrinsic immiscibility drives thin films to self-assemble into highly regular, few-nanometer-scale domains, resulting in feature sizes that are challenging to achieve with conventional lithography alone.

To harness this behavior for semiconductor device fabrication, directed self-assembly (DSA) employs predefined templates to guide polymer domains into functional patterns. However, the predominant DSA strategies, graphoepitaxy and chemoepitaxy, present challenges: graphoepitaxy confines domains within topographic trenches that can be difficult to remove or incorporate into subsequent fabrication steps, and chemoepitaxy depends on dense, nanoscale chemical patterns that are themselves challenging to fabricate.

This grant supported investigation of a new approach for the DSA of block copolymers called boundary-directed epitaxy. In this method, the boundary between two chemically different surface regions serves as a guide to position and align vertically oriented block copolymer lamellae, or nanoscale stripe-like domains. Here, we implement this concept using the edges of atomically thin graphene on germanium (Ge) as a model system. Because guidance arises from a one-dimensional boundary on an otherwise flat graphene/Ge surface, this approach avoids both the topographical features and dense, nanoscale patterns used in prior approaches.

Scientific accomplishments supported by this grant included:

  1. The development of a fabrication protocol for block copolymer self-assembly via boundary-directed epitaxy on lithographically patterned graphene templates on germanium. Unlike prior approaches that relied on randomly positioned, bottom-up synthesized graphene nanoribbons, this top-down strategy enables deterministic control over the location, orientation, density multiplication (number of repeating lamellae), and overall geometry of the self-assembled nanostructures.
  2. The establishment of a relationship between graphene boundary disorder (line-width roughness) and block copolymer assembly quality (lamellae alignment, continuity, and defect formation).
  3. The investigation of boundary-directed epitaxy on graphene templates with curved boundaries and complex shapes and the effect of bend radius on block copolymer assembly quality.
  4. The fabrication of alumina line arrays via selective alumina infiltration and etching of the assembled block copolymer structures to demonstrate an application of boundary-directed epitaxy in nanofabrication.

By clarifying how boundary roughness influences defects and by developing practical strategies to improve assembly in circuit-relevant geometries, this work addresses a key barrier to making directed self-assembly more reliable for advanced manufacturing. Such approaches that enable denser and more precisely controlled nanoscale features may support future improvements in interconnect density and energy efficiency in advanced computing hardware. Continued progress in computing performance, in turn, underpins advances across many fields, including materials science, biology, chemistry, healthcare, and more.

In addition, this project also supported broader educational and community engagement efforts, some of which are listed below:

  1. The training of PhD students, post-doctoral researchers, and a visiting professor from University of Wisconsin-Platteville, who gained technical skills in block copolymer self-assembly, characterization techniques, and advanced fabrication and processing techniques, as well as soft skills in scientific communication, presentation, and problem solving.
  2. The mentorship of two undergraduate researchers, who have continued onto PhDs in Materials Science following their graduation.
  3. The development and delivery of a public lecture for the local Madison community as part of the University of Wisconsin “Wednesday Nite @ The Lab” lecture series, titled “The Sun Is Now Ready to Make Your Electricity Greener and Cheaper in Wisconsin.”
  4. The organization of teaching demonstrations and the training of volunteers to lead hands-on scientific activities at annual outreach events, including the University of Wisconsin EXPO, Science Expeditions, Wisconsin Energy Institute Open House, and We Inspire STEM Empowerment Demo Day.

abstractText:
Advances in exosuit technologies are enabling the use of powered assistance to enhance walking performance in healthy individuals and assist individuals who exhibit gait pathologies, e.g. individuals with stroke.  Unlike rigid exoskeletons, exosuits are lightweight and use soft materials that provide a comfortable and unobtrusive fit with the body. A pack worn at the waist uses battery-powered motors to generate forces that are transmitted to the ankle and hip.  In spite of demonstrated success in decreasing the energy needed to walk, it remains challenging to tune exosuit assistance patterns for individual users. Thus, the long-term goal of this work is to enable individualized assistance that can adapt in real time to a user’s unique gait patterns and to the environment. To do this, novel sensors, termed shear wave tensiometers, will be used to track adaptations in knee and ankle muscle loading that arise when assistance is provided by a powered ankle exosuit.  Studies will be performed to determine how different exosuit assistance control patterns modulate internal muscle loading under varied walking conditions, including with  and without exosuit assistance, with and without carrying a load (backpack) and walking in an outdoor/real-world environment (declines, inclines and variable walking speeds.)  Theses studies will enhance the fundamental understanding of neuromuscular responses to exosuit assistance and thus enable human-in-the-loop implementations that adapt assistance based on the needs of an individual. Educational and outreach impact will be achieved by using fundamentals underlying the robotic, biomechanics and sensor technologies developed in this project as a platform for engaging K-12 students in STEM. Simplified versions of the exosuits and sensors will be incorporated into the annual engineering outreach event at the University of Wisconsin-Madison which reaches thousands of K-12 students and their teachers every year. Also, the Soft Robotics Toolkit hosted by Harvard will be used to create engaging content that describes human-machine interaction, biomechanics, physiology and gait.

The goal of this project is to use novel tissue load sensors, termed shear wave tensiometers, to investigate biomechanical adaptations to exosuit assistance within and beyond the laboratory environment.  Though current exosuit technologies have been shown to lower the metabolic cost of walking in healthy subjects and improve propulsion, ground clearance, and symmetry in stroke survivors, the extent of these benefits varies widely across subjects.  The project builds on a new collaboration between the lab that invented the tensiometer method to directly gauge tendon loading by measuring the propagation speed of shear waves along the tendon’s axis (University of Wisconsin-Madison) and a lab that is recognized for leadership in developing the next generation of soft exosuits (Harvard.)  The Research Plan is organized under three aims, with each aim being evaluated in 10 human subjects.  The FIRST Aim is to develop and incorporate a wearable shear wave tensiometer into an ankle exosuit to continuously monitor Achilles tendon loading during prolonged treadmill walking trials. Ankle joint torque determined from tensiometer measurements will be compared to measurements based on motion capture.  The result of this aim will be a validated wearable sensor for quantifying changes in tendon tissue loading induced by exosuit assistance.  The SECOND Aim is to evaluate relationship between ankle exosuit assistance magnitude and change in muscle-tendon loading during walking with and without added mass.  Results of this aim will provide novel insights into the relationship between exosuit assistance and biological soft tissue loads, with expectations that the tested variables (exosuit force, exosuit timing, and added mass) will have various effects on the user’s muscle-tendon load. The THIRD Aim is to evaluate the effect of ankle exosuit assistance on muscle-tendon loading while walking in an outdoor circuit that includes inclines, declines, comfortable speed and fast walking.  Measurements include tendon loading with the mobile tensiometer, muscle kinematics with ultrasound, and biomechanics and suit data with suit IMUs and load cells. Results of this aim are expected to demonstrate that, similar to how a motion capture and force plate setup in a lab environment allows for estimating joint moments, the suit sensors and tensiometer will allow for evaluating joint kinematics and tendon kinetics in outdoor environments. Success of the project is expected to lead to a new design of exosuits with integrated tensiometer sensors, produce new understanding of biomechanics with exosuits, and potentially inform optimization of personalized wearable exoskeletons for clinical and/or aged populations.

projectOutComesReport:
This project explored innovative approaches to improve wearable robotic exosuits, focusing on their ability to enhance locomotion for both healthy individuals and those with gait impairments, such as post-stroke survivors. We advanced and integrated a noninvasive sensor technology, shear wave tensiometers, that could assess how exosuits can offload muscles during human locomotion.

The intellectual merit of the project was the integration of shear wave tensiometers into wearable exosuits. These sensors provided the first feasible method for directly measuring tendon forces during walking, bypassing the limitations of traditional biomechanical models. This technology demonstrated how load carriage (15–30% of body weight) consistently increased the load requirements of the triceps surae. However, the effectiveness of ankle exosuit assistance at reducing tendon forces was variable across subjects. These results illustrate the need for personalized assistance profiles and training to make exosuits efficient.

 We conducted a pilot outdoor study that demonstrated the practicality of using shear wave tensiometers to optimize the timing and magnitude of exosuit assistance in individual subjects. The sensors were able to quickly compare different assistance patterns and zero in on most effective strategies. Tensiometer hardware and processing was improved through this project. The use of redundant accelerometers was demonstrated, with those submissions improving the reliability of tendon force measurements.

We also introduced a novel passive, self-aligning passive ankle exoskeleton that can reduce triceps surae loading during walking. This design improved comfort and function by addressing challenges associated with rigid interfaces. Testing revealed reductions in tendon loading during slow walking, though higher speeds posed challenges for consistent offloading. Future iterations will refine these designs for improved adaptability across walking speeds.

The broader impacts of this research span healthcare, mobility, and education. In a clinical context, exosuit interventions for post-stroke survivors demonstrated a shift in propulsion generation from hip-dominant strategies to increased reliance on ankle plantarflexors. This personalized adaptation underscores the potential of wearable robotics to target individual rehabilitation needs. Future optimization protocols may leverage real-time feedback mechanisms to improve mobility for individuals with neuromotor impairments, reducing energy expenditure and improving independence.

Our educational outreach activities incorporate simplified versions of the passive exosuit and sensors that were incorporated into K-12 outreach activities. These efforts emphasized biomechanics, robotics, and human-machine interaction, engaging the next generation of students pursuing STEM fields.

This project advanced the design and application of wearable robotic exosuits, offering new insights into muscle-tendon dynamics and enhancing device functionality for real-world use. By combining cutting-edge sensor technology with exosuit optimization, we laid the foundation for more effective rehabilitation tools and performance-enhancing devices, ultimately contributing to improved mobility and quality of life.

abstractText:
In this project, funded by the Chemical Structure, Dynamics, and Mechanisms A (CSDM-A) program of the Division of Chemistry, Professor Martin Zanni’s laboratory at the University of Wisconsin explores a novel property of some materials that can convert light into electricity.  In these materials, when one photon, or unit of light, hits the material, multiple electrons can carry away its electrical energy, a process known as singlet fission, whereas in most materials only one electron is excited by one photon.  Systems undergoing singlet fission can benefit the design of photovoltaic devices like solar cells and photodetectors.  Although singlet fission has been observed in crystals, the detailed mechanism by which it occurs is not established yet.  Theoretical and experimental studies show that the arrangement of molecules in a crystal plays an important role in determining electronic and charge transfer couplings that drive singlet fission.  Hence, different crystal polymorphs (i.e. different crystal packing/arrangement of the same molecule), often exhibit different singlet fission efficiencies.  By studying two model systems, this project is providing better understanding of how molecular structure, its packing into polymorphs, and its charge generation are related.  These experiments are contributing to a better understanding of how singlet fission might be utilized for more efficient charge generation.  Professor Zanni and his students also continue their involvement in educational activities, including mentoring undergraduate research students, participating in a program to provide peer-mentoring and other support for minority, low-income and first-generation graduate students, and presenting a science show and chemistry worksheet activities to local elementary schools.

Professor Zanni and his students are studying singlet fission in two molecular systems, triisopropylsilylethynyl (TIPS)-pentacene and rubrene, with the specific goal of identifying and understanding the impact of non-equilibrium structures on singlet fission. TIPS-pentacene is a solution processable organic semiconductor capable of undergoing rapid and efficient singlet fission. In previous NSF-funded work, Professor Zanni’s group revealed that TIPS-pentacene adopts different packing structure depending on the film formation procedure.  Even small changes to the crystal structure alter the interactions between two neighboring molecules, changing the electronic couplings of the singlet, triplet, and charge transfer states.  It was found that TIPS-pentacene microcrystals contain small populations of slip-stacked geometries that improve triplet state generation and also enable equilibration between the singlet and triplet states.  In this project, Professor Zanni and his group aim to extend the understanding of how spatial variation in electronic couplings through defects and polymorphs impact singlet fission and other energy transfer processes.  The slip-stacked structures are being studied by varying growth conditions, annealing, imaging crystal growth, and other experiments.  Rubrene is another material that undergoes singlet fission and crystallizes into several different polymorphs.  Singlet fission kinetics are being studied in each polymorph, in detail, to understand the relation between molecular geometry and charge transfer dynamics.  State of the art two dimensional white light (2D WL) spectroscopy and broadband transient absorption microscopy (TAM) are used for the studies.  A second-generation 2D WL microscope is being built with pulses centered in the blue part of the spectrum.  The spectral range of this new instrument allows for study of rubrene and many other important materials which absorb at shorter wavelengths than TIPS-pentacene.  This microscope is expected to enable the imaging of exciton diffusion by independently scanning the position of the pump and probe pulses.  Crystal packing and spatial heterogeneity of electronic couplings can strongly impact exciton and charge transport processes. In addition, Professor Zanni and his group assist members of the scientific community and industry in collecting and simulating 2D IR and 2D WL data, as well as participate in the educational and outreach activities discussed above.

projectOutComesReport:
The purpose of the grant was to better understand how energy flows in materials created from coupled electronic systems. One might think that energy flow is uniform, but on an atomic/molecular scale there exist defects and other heterogeneities that impact the electronic nature of materials, which in turn, impact the flow of energy. The flow of energy in materials is very important for many applications in society, including next generation solar cells and current generation light emitting devices. This proposal capitalized on a new ultrafast microscope that we invented for imaging electronic heterogeneities. The microscope generates broadband transient absorption images and sub-micron resolved 2D White-Light spectra to study the spatial dependence of energy transfer on an ultrafast timescale. Images are generated that map the energy landscape of the material, which dictates energy flow. A series of materials were imaged with the microscope, the spatial variations of excitons and biexcitons in microcrystals of a series of 2D perovskites. It was observed that the biexciton energy levels are heterogeneously distributed in the crystals, attributed to variations in environment.  The work provided a new way to identify and spatially image electronic heterogeneity, providing insight into how non-equilibrium structures influence energy transfer efficiency and timescales.

abstractText:
Molecules can be detected and identified by how they vibrate.  Their vibrations typically occur at frequencies corresponding to infrared light. Thus, by observing how molecules absorb different wavelengths of infrared light (the laboratory technique is called vibrational spectroscopy), we can tell something about their structure and properties.  However, as molecules become large (in other words “polyatomic”, meaning many atoms), or if a small molecule is surrounded by other molecules (for example, an alcohol molecule dissolved in water), their vibrations become very complicated and difficult to interpret. In this project, funded by the Chemical Structure, Dynamics and Mechanisms A of the Chemistry Division, Professor Edwin Sibert of the University of Wisconsin-Madison is extending current theoretical models in order to enhance our ability to extract structural information from the vibrations of polyatomic molecules and molecules dissolved in liquids. This research is expected to enhance our ability to interpret get a detailed picture of a molecule’s structure and its interaction with other molecules in its environment.  The models developed in this research also have implications for understanding complex biochemical processes as well as the practical design of molecules for a variety of applications, including pharmaceuticals and fuels.  Finally, the Sibert research group is also developing electronic learning resources for the undergraduate chemistry program at UW Madison.  Professor Silbert is involved in the design of electronic resources for students. These resources extend from helping students understand the forces at play in solvation phenomena to educating them about the significant contributions of chemistry to our society.

Liquid phase infrared spectra of the CH, NH and OH stretch regions often lack the spectral resolution required to interrogate how the motions of nuclei evolve upon molecular excitation. The analogous molecular motions sampled in cold clusters are governed by similar forces, yet, due to the limited cluster size and cold temperatures, the experimental spectra of these high frequency vibrations have sufficiently narrow line shapes that spectral features are revealed. The aim of this project is to provide the theoretical tools that are required for interpreting these features in order to both reveal the underlying dynamics and extract structural and environmental information. The limited size of these clusters also allows for the rigorous testing of the theoretical models. This testing includes quantifying the quality of the techniques used to determine the underlying force fields. Designing drugs and predicting outcomes of combustion reactions depend on chemists’ ability to determine such force fields in order to calculate the relative stabilities of various chemical species and understand how environment affects those stabilities. The broader impact of this project includes generating open source computer software to enable scientists to measure and understand these stabilities as well as to provide a training ground for students in this research area.

projectOutComesReport:
Our research has enhanced the information that one can obtain from studying the vibrations of molecules.  Molecules can be thought of as a collection of balls (the atoms) and springs (the bonds that hold the atoms together).  Knowing the frequency of these spring vibrations opens a window that allows us to envision the motions of the atoms of a molecule as a function of time.  Moreover, experimentalists can shine light on molecules with specific frequencies.  This light, when absorbed by the molecule, leads to excitation of specific molecular vibrations that occur at the same frequency as the light. Working closely with experimentalists, who are able to measure these vibrations for molecules that undergo a wide range of interesting molecular motions, we provide models, based on the laws of physics, that allow scientists to make the connection between the observed vibrational frequencies (a spectrum) and the motion of the atoms that results upon the molecule’s excitation (the dynamics).

Intellectual Merit.  The standard approaches for the exact modelling of molecular vibrations is computationally impossible for most interesting molecules due to their size (many degrees of freedom) and the need for quantum mechanical treatments.   The intellectual merit of our work was to recognize, that in many instances, the interesting dynamics is controlled by just a few degrees of freedom.  We then designed computer codes which included the mathematical manipulations of the exact quantum mechanical expressions in order to incorporate these approximations into our model.  Using these codes, we modelled the excitation of a variety of vibrations, enabling us to determine the molecular structures and the dynamics of 13 molecules of astronomical, chemical, and biological interest.  Specifically, modelling the spectra of OH and NH stretches provided information as to how low-frequency vibrations respond to the excitation of these stretches. This work required skill in evaluating the quality of electronic structure methods, running molecular dynamics, and finding approximate solutions to the time-dependent and -independent nuclear Schrodinger equations for modeling the nuclear motion of the molecule that is being probed experimentally.  Comparing model results to experimental spectra provided rigorous tests of the accuracy of the potential force fields that are used as input to the models.  We also published two papers that focused on improving the mathematical tools used in underlying the theoretical models of vibrations as well as a review article describing the current status of the field.

Broader Impacts.   An overarching outcome of our research was to improve chemist’s ability to predict the nuclear motions of atoms and molecules over a broad range of environments. These predictions will form the basis for the better design of products that are important to society such as drugs and batteries.  The sound mentoring and support of graduate students and a post doc, as they develop as chemists, has provided our society individuals that will continue to advance chemical knowledge in either industry or academia.  Working as an educator and administrator of large STEM classes, the PI was involved in the planning of curricula and the associated resources.  These resources extend from helping students understand the forces at play in solvation phenomena to educating them about the significant contributions of chemistry to our society.

abstractText:
Cave habitats are remarkable environments for the study of biological adaptations and morphological convergence. One compelling trait that has repeatedly evolved in cave-dwelling organisms is loss of the eyes. Predatory arthropods like arachnids (e.g., spiders and harvestmen) play an important role in cave ecosystems and the group includes many examples of cave-adapted blind species. However, remarkably little is known about how arachnid eyes develop, much less how these eyes are lost in cave-specialized arachnids. This binational project brings together a US-Israeli team to advance understanding the evolutionary developmental biology of arachnid eyes. To examine how eyes are lost in cave-adapted arachnids, embryonic development will be compared for a sister-species pair in each of three arachnid orders (spiders, whip spiders, and harvestmen) that will be collected through intensive fieldwork campaigns; in each pair, a surface species bears eyes and its sister species is blind. To determine the genomic basis for eye degeneration, high-quality reference genomes will be established for these six species, together with profiling of gene expression using parallelized short read sequencing. To validate predictions of key genes putatively underlying cave adaptations that are inferred from genomic datasets, gene silencing screens will be performed in two model arachnid species, with the goal of establishing a direct link between patterns observed in nature and functional datasets in the laboratory. 
 
By comparison to better-studied vertebrate and pancrustacean (e.g., insects; isopod crustaceans) models, eye development in Chelicerata remains poorly studied. With respect to the developmental genetics of arachnid eyes, no datasets are available beyond in situ hybridization assays; even the morphogenesis of arachnid eyes remains underexplored from the perspective of modern imaging toolkits, relative to vertebrate and pancrustacean counterparts. Yet, the arachnid eye is of interest from the standpoint of comparative biology for two reasons. First, in contrast to the main pair of compound (faceted) eyes of pancrustaceans, arachnids bear multiple eye pairs broadly divided into two types of ocelli, which are structurally and functionally distinct from each other. A further complexity of arachnids is that a subset of orders that includes lineages like scorpions and spiders has undergone a shared genome duplication, resulting in numerous paralogs of retinal determinal gene network (RDGN) homologs, which are involved in patterning eyes of many other bilaterian groups. The proposed work will interrogate the development of arachnid eyes using a comparative framework that samples three key arachnid orders, toward establishing a comparative platform incorporating independently evolving lineages for study of cave biology, as well as for understanding the evolution of paralog function after genome duplication. Beyond establishing new model systems for study of arthropod development, this research will establish new genomic resources and toolkits for deciphering the evolution of developmental processes inferred from naturally evolving cave systems.

This research award from the Directorate of Biological Sciences is funded by the Developmental Systems and EDGE Programs within the Division of Integrative and Organismal Systems, and by the Evolutionary Processes Program within the Division of Environmental Biology.

projectOutComesReport:
Arachnid eye development is of interest from a comparative standpoint for two reasons. First, arachnid eyes are structurally and functionally different from those of vertebrates or pancrustaceans. Second, a subdivision of arachnids that includes spiders has undergone ancient genome duplication, with retention of numerous duplicates of developmental patterning genes. Gene expression assays have suggested that several paralogs of eye-patterning genes have subdivided their ancestral homologs’ functions in spiders, as inferred from non-overlapping expression domains of duplicated transcription factors in different pairs of eyes. This inference was untested, as no functional genetic data existed for eye formation in any arachnid.

To bridge this knowledge gap, we pursued an enhanced understanding of how arachnid eyes become vestigial and are ultimately lost. Though joint fieldwork efforts, we generated developmental transcriptomes from embryos of eye-bearing and blind sister species of Israeli arachnids. Bioinformatic analyses of these samples revealed that specific duplicated copies of genes in the retinal determination network (RDN)—a broadly conserved gene network that is required for eye patterning across bilaterian animals—were differentially expressed in the eye-bearing versus the reduced-eye species. To test the function of these bioinformatically identified candidates, we performed gene silencing against the orthologs of these genes in the tractable spider model Parasteatoda tepidariorum. We discovered that knockdown of one copy of sine oculis (so-1) resulted in disruption of both median and lateral eye pairs in developing spider embryos, consistent with the result of the differential gene expression analysis of blind and eye-bearing arachnid sister species in nature. This outcome constituted the first functional data point informing eye development in any arachnid species. 

We then turned to characterization of RDN gene function during eye development in the daddy-longlegs (order Opiliones) Phalangium opilio, a species with an unduplicated genome and which is highly responsive to gene silencing experiments. In contrast to groups like spiders and scorpions that have both a pair of median eyes and several pairs of lateral eyes, daddy-longlegs were thought to possess a single eye pair as a result of evolutionary loss of the lateral eyes. We unexpectedly discovered that P. opilio has not one, but three pairs of r-opsin-positive organs in the developing head. We inferred that two of these pairs comprised a vestigial median eye pair and a vestigial lateral eye pair. To test this hypothesis, we studied the neuroanatomy of the embryonic harvestman brain. We confirmed our hypothesis that two different neuropils innervate the median and lateral eye systems. Next, we performed RNA interference against the gene eyes absent and showed that disruption of this eye-patterning gene resulted in loss of all three eye pairs, corroborating the identity of these organs as vestigial eyes. To test the identity of the lateral pair as vestigial lateral eyes, we performed RNA interference against the gene dachshund. Consistent with our prediction, disruption of dachshund resulted in the deletion of the lateral eyes, but not the two median eye pairs. Taken together, our results showed that daddy-longlegs have a plesiomorphic eye architecture that is more comparable to that of horseshoe crabs than to arachnid groups like spiders. This result changed the understanding of eye evolution in Chelicerata and Arachnida. We also showed that the discovery of these additional eye pairs dramatically changes the placement of the oldest Opiliones fossils, underscoring the value of developmental genetic datasets in our understanding of evolutionary history.

The outcomes of this award have substantially impacted our understanding of eye development and evolution in the arachnids. At the time of this writing, our team has generated fully all the functional datasets informing eye development in Chelicerata.  Resources generated under this project include developmental transcriptomes and genomes for phylogenetically significant arthropod groups, including the first genome of an Opiliones, a whip spider, and a whip scorpion. These resources have additionally informed our understanding of the phylogeny of Chelicerata, with downstream implications for the history of terrestrialization, as well as corroborated the incidence of a whole genome duplication event uniting the clade Arachnopulmonata (a group of arachnid orders that includes spiders and scorpions). These studies have transformed our present understanding of chelicerate evolution.

The impact of this work is noticeable in modern teaching and public resources. As a concrete example, the most recent edition of Invertebrates (Brusca et al., 4th edition), a definitive text commonly used across college campuses, now features results of this award in its overview of chelicerate evolution, as well as in two of the chapter’s figures. In addition, results of this research are featured on multiple Wikipedia pages.

This award supported the training of three postdoctoral researchers, four graduate students, and 16 undergraduate students. Additional activities supported by this award include outreach events targeting K-12 students, teaching modules developed for AP Biology classrooms, dissemination of research outcomes at scientific conferences, and binational collaboration and training visits between US and Israeli research institutions.

abstractText:
Unsupervised learning can be described as the task of finding structure from unlabeled observations. This is a fundamental task in scientific fields like biology, material science, economics, and astronomy, where in a typical scenario researchers possess a large number of unlabeled data, but only a few (or none) expert labeled data points, as these are typically very expensive to obtain. This project focuses on the mathematical analysis of data science algorithms for unsupervised learning. Broadly speaking, the aim of the investigation is to contribute to the development of mathematical foundations for data science and artificial intelligence by providing rigorous mathematical theory supporting methodologies used in practice, as well as by proposing principled novel ones. The investigator will not only study individual algorithms, but find common structure between them and highlight their otherwise unclear unity.

Among the many methodologies for unsupervised learning found in the literature, graph-based methods occupy a prominent role, and they will be the focus of this investigation. These are algorithms that rely on having access to similarity graphs, which endow data sets with a geometric structure. Different graphs capture different features of a given data set and hence are useful for different tasks. The project will focus on the following concrete directions: 1) the proposal and analysis of new algorithms for unsupervised learning inspired by variational methods for evolution on metric spaces and in particular on the space of probability measures over discrete and semi-discrete structures. In this direction the main goal is to introduce a mathematical formalism for the design of new learning methodologies, and to use this formalism in order to build connections between seemingly unrelated statistical procedures like those inspired by mode-seeking techniques as the ones based on spectral methods. Some of the applications in mind go beyond unsupervised learning, and also include the systematic testing of deep neural network architectures. The second direction concerns the study of statistical properties of graph-based unsupervised learning algorithms in settings where graphs capturing the geometry of a data set are very sparse (below standard connectivity), or where data generating distributions are degenerate and violate standard geometric assumptions found in the literature. In this direction, the goal is to identify the limits of sparsity that allow for meaningful learning, as well as to develop quantitative statistical error analysis for solutions to non-convex optimization problems on graphs built on data sets, for graphs that are connected to a ground truth geometric model.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
With the widespread use of machine learning and data analysis methodologies across various application domains in recent years, there has been an increased interest in the scientific community to unveil the mathematical principles underlying these methods. In this project, the PI and his collaborators explored a range of methodologies in data science and machine learning with a common theme: a close connection to optimization problems over geometric objects and/or association with partial differential equations, which traditionally are used to describe physical phenomena like heat propagation. The link between data analysis algorithms, on the one hand, and equations and optimization problems typically found in mathematical analysis or geometry, on the other, is an important theme across the project. This interaction between seemingly unrelated topics has also inspired the proposal of new algorithms in data science with theoretical guarantees.

In more concrete terms, the PI and his collaborators established new theoretical foundations for graph-based clustering in mathematical settings that better resemble real-life application scenarios than previous theoretical studies; clustering, in this context, refers to identifying relevant group structures in datasets. They also provided new theoretical insights for unsupervised learning methodologies such as diffusion maps, and they proposed new forms of interpolation between density-driven and geometry-based unsupervised learning algorithms, two well-known general perspectives in the machine learning literature for unsupervised learning (including clustering), providing in this way further mathematical insights into traditionally unrelated methodologies.

As part of the project, the PI and collaborators used the opportunity to present the theoretical foundations of graph-based semi-supervised learning in an expository article. Semi-supervised learning, closely related to unsupervised learning, involves having additional "label" information for some data points within a larger collection of data. The tools discussed in that manuscript heavily rely on variational techniques, specifically on the variational formulation of posterior updates in Bayesian statistics.

The project also delved into studying path distances and curvature in datasets and establishing their close relation to analogous notions on more standard geometric objects like spheres or flat surfaces. The implications of these analytical results on unsupervised and supervised learning methodologies were discussed by the PI and collaborators, and in particular, they support the use of data-driven “curvature” constraints in learning representations for data.

The PI and collaborators also proposed new methods for finding suitable "neural architectures" in supervised learning problems, aiming to identify the best tool within a class of existing tools to solve a given learning problem.

Furthermore, the project played a crucial role in paving the way for new and profound explorations of the theoretical foundations of adversarial machine learning in supervised classification settings. Adversarial machine learning, an area of modern machine learning, focuses on studying and developing methods to construct learning models that are robust to adversarial perturbations of data. These problems are particularly relevant in various safety-critical applications, aligning with the overarching goal of making data analysis and machine algorithms safe, fair, and robust.

In addition to the aforementioned research outcomes, the project was essential in developing several topic courses for graduate students at the PI’s institution. These courses contributed to the formation of a new generation of researchers at the interface between mathematics, statistics, and machine learning. Three new PhD students joined the PI in the research endeavors prompted by this project, along with multiple Master’s students who participated in weekly reading groups and extracurricular discussion sessions on the role that mathematics can play in the development of data science.

abstractText:
Single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) are an emerging sensor technology capable of detecting individual incident photons and capturing their time-of-arrival with picosecond precision. Due to their high sensitivity and time resolution, SPADs are driving an imaging revolution, enabling extreme applications that were hitherto considered impossible: imaging at trillion frames-per-second, non-line-of-sight imaging, and microscopic imaging at nano time-scales. Despite these capabilities, SPADs are considered specialized devices used only in ultra-dark environments and restricted to a limited set of niche applications. This project develops technologies to expand the scope of SPADs as general-purpose cameras with a broad range of applications. The developed technologies will not only spur wide-spread adoption of SPADs in fields like life science, astronomy, and medicine, where operating with the smallest amount of light possible is critical to success, but also enable new, highly demanding applications. 3D cameras will be able to achieve substantially higher depth resolution than current state-of-the-art at long distances, enabling vehicles (aerial, terrestrial, and underwater) to navigate autonomously in challenging weather conditions and on rugged terrains. The results from this research will be disseminated through scientific conferences and journals. Some materials will be integrated into a textbook on active 3D imaging techniques. 

This research develops mathematical and physical foundations for a new class of imaging and computational techniques which will transform SPADs into `all-purpose' cameras capable of operating in diverse conditions (dark to bright sunlight), for recovering high-quality images and 3D scene information over the entire gamut of imaging conditions. This project develops (a) coded and asynchronous single-photon imaging, two novel families of active single-photon imaging techniques that minimize non-linear distortions and can reliably operate in high-flux environments; (b) single-photon computational imaging techniques for capturing scene intensity under passive, uncontrolled lighting (e.g., sunlight); and (c) novel machine learning algorithms for extracting high-level scene information from single-photon sensor data, based on spiking neural networks, enabling rapid, power-efficient scene understanding in dynamic environments, on low-power devices.

abstractText:
The project will develop a sustainable and scalable approach to train a workforce skilled in research and application of machine learning (ML) in materials informatics. ML in materials informatics is rapidly transforming materials science and engineering (MS&E) by an unprecedented ability to extend materials databases, improve materials simulation, mine texts, automate materials research and development, and accelerate materials design. As pointed out by multiple recent studies, including from the National Academies and the Minerals, Metals & Materials Society (TMS), it is essential to train a next generation workforce in ML for materials informatics to realize its enormous potential for improving the human condition through advanced materials. Unfortunately, ML in materials informatics is almost completely absent from today's materials curricula at the undergraduate level. However, the power of informatics tools combined with their rapid evolution and relative novelty in MS&E creates an opportunity for engaging undergraduates (UGs) with active learning through impactful research. With this motivation, the project will create new infrastructure and an ecosystem for the engagement and training of UGs across the U.S. in research using applied ML in materials informatics, called the Informatics Skunkworks. The Skunkworks consists of mentor/UG teams performing research in materials informatics. The project provides the teams with new resources, consisting of curricula, software, and research problems, and with a community of practice to support research and to work effectively and collaboratively. The low cost and accessibility of ML and materials informatics creates an opportunity for Skunkworks to engage mentors and students with limited research resources, particularly at institutions serving underrepresented groups. The Skunkworks is a sustainable and scalable approach that can fulfill this unmet need by training a diverse workforce skilled in research and application of ML for materials informatics. 
   
The project will provide freely available (a) curriculum to train UGs in relevant ML, materials informatics and research professional development, (b) software tools that augment existing ML packages to be UG accessible, and (c) authentic and appropriate-level research problems. The proposed work will also develop a community of practice to enable a network of productive mentor/UG research teams to effectively and collaboratively use the curricular, software and other resources developed by the project to support transforming the future workforce. The intellectual merit of the proposed work is to (a) develop scalable resources to increase UG experience and learning in research at the boundary of data science and materials science and engineering, (b) grow a community of mentors and UG researchers engaged in materials informatics research, and (c) increase the utilization of data science tools for solving critical problems in MS&E and related fields through workforce development and materials informatics training. The broader impact of the proposed work is to (a) freely disseminate enabling curricula and tools for materials informatics, (b) train staff, mentors and UGs in broadly applicable research and professional skills, and (c) develop a diverse community of practice for materials informatics researchers. The project will enable the development of a new workforce capable of advanced materials informatics, especially for underrepresented groups, by supporting primarily UG institutions and community colleges that often have limited research resources. This project is funded by the Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure in the Directorate for Computer and Information Science and Engineering, with the Division of Materials Research in the Directorate for Mathematical and Physical Sciences also contributing funds.

projectOutComesReport:
Overview: The Informatics Skunkworks Program increased undergraduate participation in research at the interface of data science and materials science. To do this we lowered barriers to participation and developed program resources that supported effective mentoring of large groups of students. Specific activities were: (1) developing educational resources, including a modular curriculum, software tools, and undergraduate research projects, and (2) fostering a collaborative community to support both students and mentors. The program has trained over 600 students from over 30 institutions.

Key Accomplishments:

  1. Development of Educational Resources: One major challenge to undergraduate research participation is learning both the technical and professional skills students need to succeed. The program developed and maintained a set of resources that were taught by program mentors as a one semester course to onboard new students. This included modular educational content, hands-on activities, and tutorials on machine learning topics, such as model assessment, deep learning, and uncertainty quantification. The curriculum, designed to be accessible to undergraduates from any location and background, made use of cloud computing platforms like Google Colab, ensuring widespread usability without the need for local computational resources.
  2. Expansion of Undergraduate Research Opportunities: Throughout the program, numerous undergraduate research projects were conducted, engaging students from institutions across the U.S. and internationally. Research projects covered a wide range of topics in data science and materials science, with mentorship provided by faculty and staff from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Boise State University. To increase student participation, resources and project structures were developed that enabled group-based research where ~10 students can effectively contribute to one project instead of the traditional one-student one-mentor model. As project mentors are usually the limiting factor for engagement of undergraduates, this more scalable approach increased participation numbers by about an order of magnitude.
  3. Building a National and International Community: The program successfully built a vibrant community through regular connecting events, including virtual help desks, mentor check-ins, workshops, and hybrid "All-Hands" meetings. This community was supported by online platforms such as Slack, which facilitated collaboration and communication across institutions. Due to the structure of the educational course as well as the research projects, students were able to effectively contribute to projects from any location without a need for local computing resources. This delocalization had great success in reaching institutions which traditionally would not be able to offer research opportunities to their students.
  4. Professional Development: The program also provided significant professional development opportunities, including workshops on responsible conduct in machine learning research, scientific communication, and hands-on sessions on state-of-the-art tools such as large language models. Students participating in the program reported improved research skills, increased confidence in machine learning applications, and a stronger connection to the materials science research community.

Broader Impacts: This program made a dramatic impact on both undergraduate education through the direct training of over 600 students and the development of resources and methods that can support this type of training format in the future. By developing resources that lower the barriers for students to engage in undergraduate research, the Informatics Skunkworks program has contributed to workforce development in materials science and data science. Furthermore, the program's success in building diverse, multi-institutional engagement sets a model for how effective undergraduate research can be conducted in a virtual, collaborative environment.

The project has also played a key role in the professional development of mentors and researchers, helping to bridge the gap between education and research applications. The ongoing use and development of the MAST-ML software tool for machine learning in materials science has enhanced both research and educational outcomes. Overall this program has helped ensure that students are well-equipped with the skills needed to thrive in the growing field of data-driven materials science.

abstractText:
This award is supported by the Major Research Instrumentation and the Chemistry Research Instrumentation programs. The University of Wisconsin Madison is acquiring a 500 MHz nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer equipped with a flow tube accessory and dedicated software that enable online monitoring of chemical reactions in real-time under actual experimental conditions. The instrumentation supports Professor Charles Fry and colleagues at the Wisconsin High-Pressure Reactor (WiHP-NNMR). This spectrometer allows research in a variety of fields such as those that accelerate chemical reactions of significant economic importance, as well as permitting study of biologically relevant species. In general, NMR spectroscopy is one of the most powerful tools available to chemists for the elucidation of the structure of molecules. It is used to identify unknown substances, to characterize specific arrangements of atoms within molecules, and to study the dynamics of interactions between molecules in solution or in the solid state. Access to state-of-the-art NMR spectrometers is essential to chemists who are carrying out frontier research. This instrument is an integral part of teaching as well as research and research training of undergraduate students in chemistry and biochemistry at this institution and nearby colleges such as Madison College, University of Wisconsin La Crosse, University of Wisconsin Rock County, University of Wisconsin Whitewater, Lawrence University, Maranatha Baptist University, Indiana State University and Valparaiso University. The Magnetic Resonance Facility plays an important role in strengthening the relationship between the University and Wisconsin citizens by working closely with departmental programs advocating the importance of science, research, and education to the public.

The award of the NMR spectrometer is aimed at enhancing research and education at all levels. It especially impacts discovery of metal-metal bonded catalysts and carbon-hydrogen functionalization reactions. The instrumentation is also for exploring photoredox catalysis, polymer mechanochemistry and three-dimensional (3D) printing. In addition, it provides information on operando investigations of transition metal catalyzed reactions. An operando method involves spectroscopic characterization of materials undergoing reaction which is coupled simultaneously with measurement of catalytic activity and selectivity. The spectrometer is also used to develop catalysts for aerobic oxidation.
